chapter.name: How Nature Works in Harmony
chapter.blurb: Starting from the story of elephants entering farms and villages as their forest habitats shrink, this chapter builds from habitats and their biotic and abiotic components, to populations and communities, the different kinds of interactions among organisms and their surroundings, food chains and food webs built on producers, consumers and decomposers, how one small change can cascade through an ecosystem, competition and relationships such as mutualism, commensalism and parasitism that keep ecosystems in dynamic balance, and finally the benefits ecosystems such as the Sundarbans mangrove forest provide, protected areas, and how sustainable farming can help keep this balance intact.

scope_in.item: Opening example: habitat loss forcing elephants into farms and villages, and wildlife corridors
Habitat definition and biotic and abiotic components, with pond and forest examples (Table 12.1)
Population definition with the numeric garden-count example; community definition; flower parts and pollination
Case study: fish, dragonflies and pollinators in Pond A versus Pond B, and direct and indirect effects
Types of interactions - biotic-abiotic, abiotic-abiotic, and biotic-biotic - with Table 12.3 examples
Ecosystem definition; aquatic versus terrestrial ecosystems; overlapping ecosystems; hierarchy from individual to ecosystem; biotic components affecting abiotic ones
Producers/autotrophs and consumers/heterotrophs; herbivores, carnivores and omnivores, with Table 12.4 examples
Food chains, trophic levels and food webs
Decomposers, decomposition and the recycling of nutrients
Cascading effects of a small change in an ecosystem - the pond pollution example
Case study: decline of frog populations from frog-leg export and the 1980s export ban
Ecosystem balance as dynamic, not fixed; competition for resources controlling population size
Mutualism, commensalism and parasitism with named examples; A.J.T. Johnsingh's predator-prey research in Bandipur National Park
Benefits of ecosystems to humans; the Sundarbans - location, protection role, UNESCO status and threats
Protected areas - types and named examples across India
Human-made ecosystems - fish ponds, farms and parks
India's food crisis and the Green Revolution; why these farming methods are now considered unsustainable, and their effects on soil, pests and biodiversity; Vrikshayurveda and organic manure

concepts.name: Habitats and their biotic and abiotic components
concepts.description: A habitat provides the living and non-living conditions an organism needs to survive; habitats such as ponds and forests have both biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) components, and shrinking habitats can force animals like elephants into farms and villages.
concepts.idea: Every habitat has biotic components (living things) and abiotic components (non-living things) that together decide the conditions organisms experience there.
concepts.rule: A habitat is the place where an organism lives and gets everything it needs to survive; it could be as large as a forest or as small as the bark of a tree. Every habitat has biotic components, which are the living beings in it such as plants, animals and microbes, and abiotic components, which are the non-living things in it such as air, water, soil, sunlight and temperature. In a pond habitat, fish, frogs, turtles, snakes, dragonflies, algae and lotus are biotic components, while water and soil are abiotic components. A pond provides food, oxygen, shelter and space to grow, which are conditions essential for survival; fish get biotic needs such as food from small plants and animals, and abiotic needs such as oxygen from the water. Different habitats offer different living conditions, so different organisms live in each one. Even within a single habitat, physical conditions such as air, sunlight, water, temperature and soil can vary; for example, a forest may be warm during the day and cool at night, so a snake that comes out at night and a rodent active during the day face different conditions even though they share the same habitat, and this is how living organisms coexist in harmony. Loss of forest cover, changes in rainfall, and cutting trees for roads and buildings shrink habitats and force animals such as elephants to enter farms and villages in search of food; wildlife ecologists mark corridors that connect forest habitats so animals can move safely between them without conflict with human settlements.
concepts.example: A pond habitat has biotic components such as fish, frogs and algae, and abiotic components such as water and soil, while shrinking forest habitats are forcing elephants into farms in some Indian states.

concepts.name: Populations, communities, and why every organism matters
concepts.description: A population is a group of the same kind of organism in a habitat, and different populations sharing a habitat form a community; the Pond A versus Pond B study shows how a change in one population can affect others through direct and indirect effects.
concepts.idea: Populations of different kinds together form a community, and a change to one population in a community can have direct and indirect effects on others.
concepts.rule: A population is a group of organisms of the same kind living together in a habitat at a given time, such as all the fish of one kind in a pond, or 20 plants of one type counted in a 1 metre by 1 metre patch of garden compared to only 5 plants of another type in the same patch. A community comprises the different populations that share the same habitat; the biotic components of a habitat, such as its plants, animals and microorganisms, together form the community, and these organisms interact with and depend on one another for survival. A flower has a stalk, sepals, petals and two reproductive parts, the carpels (female) and the stamens (male); stamens release pollen, which wind, water, insects, bats and birds carry to the carpels of the same or different flowers in a process called pollination, which is essential for the formation of fruits and seeds. Researchers compared Pond A, which had fish and many flowering plants around it, with Pond B, which had no fish and fewer flowering plants. Pond A had fewer dragonflies than Pond B because fish eat dragonfly larvae; with fewer dragonflies, which normally eat bees, flies and butterflies, more of these pollinating insects survived in Pond A, helping pollinate more flowers, so flowers near Pond A produced more seeds. This shows how one biotic component, fish, can have a direct effect on another, dragonflies, and an indirect effect on pollinators and seed production, showing that every organism in a community matters.
concepts.example: In Pond A, fish reduce the number of dragonflies by eating their larvae, which indirectly leaves more bees and butterflies to pollinate flowers, so more seeds are produced near Pond A than near Pond B.

concepts.name: Types of interactions and the ecosystem
concepts.description: Interactions in a habitat can be biotic-abiotic, abiotic-abiotic or biotic-biotic; the interaction of biotic and abiotic components together forms an ecosystem, and organisms are organised from individual to population to community to ecosystem.
concepts.idea: Biotic and abiotic components interact with each other in three ways, and their combined interaction in a habitat forms an ecosystem.
concepts.rule: Interactions in a habitat can be grouped into three kinds: interactions between abiotic and biotic components, such as earthworms living in moist soil or a fish laying eggs in water; interactions between two abiotic components, such as sunlight making the day temperature high, or air currents creating gentle waves on a pond's surface; and interactions among biotic components, such as a frog eating insects, a water snake eating fish, or frogs and fish competing for the same insect larvae. The interaction of the biotic components (plants, animals and microorganisms) and the abiotic components (air, water, soil, sunlight and temperature) of a habitat together forms an ecosystem. There are two main types of ecosystems: aquatic ecosystems, such as ponds, rivers and lakes, and terrestrial ecosystems, such as forests, farms or even a single large tree; a farmland is a human-made terrestrial ecosystem. Ecosystems can overlap, for example a river running alongside mountains, forests, grassland and farmland in the same area. In an ecosystem, sunlight, carbon dioxide and water are essential for plants to make food, soil gives nutrients for growth, air gives oxygen for respiration, and water is essential for all living organisms, showing how biotic components depend on abiotic components. The reverse is also true: biotic components influence abiotic ones, since plants release oxygen during photosynthesis, their roots hold soil in place and prevent erosion, and plants retain soil moisture and help cool the atmosphere. Organisms are organised in levels: an individual belongs to a population, populations of different kinds together form a community, and a community interacting with its abiotic components forms an ecosystem.
concepts.example: Earthworms living in moist soil is an interaction between a biotic component and an abiotic component, while a frog eating insects is an interaction between two biotic components.

concepts.name: Producers, consumers, decomposers, food chains and food webs
concepts.description: Plants (producers) make their own food, consumers depend on other organisms for food as herbivores, carnivores or omnivores, food chains show who eats whom through trophic levels, interlinked chains form food webs, and decomposers recycle nutrients from dead matter.
concepts.idea: Organisms are linked through feeding relationships - producers, consumers and decomposers - forming food chains, trophic levels and food webs.
concepts.rule: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis, so they are called producers or autotrophs (auto = self, troph = food). Organisms that cannot make their own food and depend on other organisms for it are called consumers or heterotrophs (hetero = other, troph = food). Consumers that eat only plants are herbivores, such as deer and hare; those that eat only animals are carnivores, such as leopard and vulture; those that eat both plants and animals are omnivores, such as crows, foxes and mice. A food chain is a simple sequence showing who eats whom in an ecosystem, such as grass eaten by a hare, which is eaten by a leopard, or grass eaten by a grasshopper, which is eaten by a frog, which is eaten by a snake, which is eaten by an eagle. Each organism's position in a food chain is called a trophic level: producers such as green plants are at the first trophic level, herbivores such as hares and deer are at the second trophic level, small carnivores such as frogs are at the third trophic level, and large carnivores such as tigers or vultures occupy the next trophic level. Since an organism may be eaten by more than one kind of organism, food chains in an ecosystem are interlinked into a network called a food web. Living organisms produce waste, including dead matter, during their lives. Microorganisms such as fungi (for example mushrooms growing on dead wood) and bacteria break down this complex dead matter into simpler substances in a process called decomposition, returning nutrients to the soil; these organisms are called decomposers or saprotrophs (sapro = rotten, troph = food).
concepts.example: In the food chain grass, hare, leopard, the grass is a producer, the hare is a herbivore at the second trophic level, and the leopard is a carnivore.

concepts.name: Ecological balance: cascading change, competition and relationships between organisms
concepts.description: A small change can cascade through an ecosystem, as in the pond pollution and frog-leg export examples; ecosystem balance is dynamic and kept in check by competition and by relationships such as mutualism, commensalism and parasitism.
concepts.idea: Ecosystems stay in dynamic balance through competition and relationships among organisms, and a single change can cascade into many further effects.
concepts.rule: A small change in an ecosystem can lead to a chain of other changes. For example, if pollution kills plants in a pond, less oxygen is produced in the water, which can cause the fish population to drop; with fewer fish to eat them, insects increase in number and may spread to nearby farmland, forcing farmers to use pesticides, which can further harm the environment. In the 1980s, India exported large numbers of frog legs, especially of the Indian bullfrog (Hoplobatrachus tigerinus); this large-scale harvesting reduced frog populations, and since frogs eat insects, fewer frogs led to a rise in agricultural pests, forcing farmers to use more synthetic pesticides, which harmed the environment, soil, water and human health, so the Government of India banned the export of frog legs to prevent further ecological damage. An ecosystem stays in balance when interactions among organisms and their environment keep populations and resources stable; this balance is dynamic, not fixed, and can be disrupted by natural or human-made changes. Organisms also compete for common resources such as food, water, physical space or sunlight; this competition helps control population size and keeps the ecosystem balanced, since without it one species could multiply too much and cause an imbalance. Organisms also form other kinds of relationships: in mutualism, both organisms benefit, such as honeybees and flowers; in commensalism, one organism benefits while the other is not affected, such as orchids growing on trees; in parasitism, one organism benefits while the other is harmed, such as ticks feeding on the blood of dogs. The Indian wildlife biologist A.J.T. Johnsingh studied forest ecosystems using modern tracking methods; his research in Bandipur National Park, Karnataka, showed how predators such as tigers and leopards depend on prey such as deer and wild boar, and that a healthy prey population is key to predator survival.
concepts.example: Banning the export of frog legs in the 1980s helped protect frog populations and reduce the rise in agricultural pests caused by their decline.

concepts.name: Ecosystem benefits, human-made ecosystems and sustainable farming
concepts.description: Ecosystems such as the Sundarbans provide humans with resources and protection, protected areas conserve wildlife, humans also build ecosystems such as farms and fish ponds, and unsustainable farming methods such as overusing fertilisers and pesticides can harm soil and biodiversity.
concepts.idea: Ecosystems provide many benefits to people, but human-made ecosystems and farming practices must be managed sustainably to avoid harming the balance they depend on.
concepts.rule: Ecosystems benefit humans in many ways: forests provide fresh air, fertile soil, food, fibres, timber and medicines, aquatic ecosystems provide water and food, and ecosystems also have aesthetic and recreational value. The Sundarbans has the largest mangrove forest in the world, located where the Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers meet between India and Bangladesh; its forests and rivers are home to many endangered species, and the mangroves protect people by slowing down strong winds and waves during storms and floods, while its trees absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen. UNESCO declared the Sundarbans a World Heritage Site in 1987, but it faces threats from mangroves being cut for fuelwood and farming, illegal hunting, overuse of forest resources, and pollution from industrial waste and untreated sewage. Protected areas are parts of land or water set aside to conserve wildlife and habitats, and include national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves and community conserved areas, such as Jim Corbett National Park in Uttarakhand, Manas National Park in Assam, the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve in the Western Ghats, Chilika Lake in Odisha, Eaglenest Wildlife Sanctuary in Arunachal Pradesh, Hemis National Park in Leh, Keibul Lamjao National Park in Manipur, and Pirotan Island Marine National Park in Gujarat. Humans also create artificial or human-made ecosystems such as fish ponds, farms and parks; when well designed, these can help reduce pollution, support biodiversity and provide recreational spaces, but unlike natural ecosystems they need human care and management. India faced a food crisis between 1950 and 1965 due to low crop production; the Green Revolution in the mid-20th century used tractors, machines, synthetic fertilisers and pesticides to increase food production. However, these methods are now considered unsustainable because overusing synthetic fertilisers can reduce soil fertility by decreasing friendly soil microorganisms and lowering humus, which leaves soil prone to erosion, and by reducing natural predators, which increases pest populations. Heavy irrigation and repeated ploughing can disturb soil organisms such as earthworms and snails, some pests develop resistance to pesticides, and growing the same crop repeatedly, called monoculture, can reduce biodiversity and affect pollinators. The ancient Indian text Vrikshayurveda emphasises soil health through organic manure such as Kunapa Jala, a liquid fertiliser made by fermenting animal and plant waste.

questions.q: Compare a natural ecosystem and a human-made ecosystem, using an example of each.
questions.a: A natural ecosystem, such as a forest, forms and sustains itself without human management; a human-made ecosystem, such as a fish pond or farm, is created by people and needs ongoing human care and management.

questions.q: Explain how the Vrikshayurveda's emphasis on organic manure like Kunapa Jala connects to the problems caused by overusing synthetic fertilisers described in the chapter.
questions.a: Overusing synthetic fertilisers can reduce friendly soil microorganisms and humus, making soil prone to erosion, while the ancient text Vrikshayurveda instead promotes continuously nourishing soil with organic manures like Kunapa Jala, made by fermenting animal and plant waste, showing an older sustainable approach to the same problem of maintaining soil health.

questions.q: Do you think protected areas like national parks are enough on their own to protect India's ecosystems? Justify your answer.
questions.a: A reasoned answer either way is acceptable, for example that protected areas help conserve specific habitats and species, but sustainable farming and reducing pollution elsewhere are also needed to protect ecosystems more broadly.

questions.q: Design a short set of sustainable farming practices a farmer could adopt to reduce the problems caused by overusing synthetic fertilisers and pesticides, based on the chapter.
questions.a: For example: rotate crops instead of relying on monoculture, use organic manure such as compost, reduce excessive irrigation, and encourage natural predators of pests instead of relying only on synthetic pesticides.
s: Linked to reducing a named problem
